Another teammate was working at the same time in the branch remotes/origin/vlad, can you compare what both branches account for and tell me if A. One of them is overall better than the other and accounts for more stuff (Like using Clef for quick decisions on screenshot to skip Captchas instead of calling Qwen) B. They have a disjoint set of features that would require a thoughful merge

I’ll compare the two implementations as they stand, focusing on architecture, capability coverage, test evidence, and whether the differences are complementary or conflicting. I’ll keep this read-only and won’t merge or modify either branch.

`fresh-start` is substantially more complete for the requested EHL Atira outcome. Vlad’s branch is a focused investigation MVP, while `fresh-start` implements the full bid lifecycle.

| Area | `fresh-start` | `origin/vlad` |
|---|---|---|
| Browser design | One controller / one browser, matching the stated default | Up to four parallel investigators / browsers |
| Evidence | Typed, scoped, conflict-aware ledger with document handling | In-memory quoted evidence ledger |
| RFQ rules and pricing | Implemented with `Decimal`, allocation, revisions, stock, discount, setup, bonus, etc. | Documented as future work only |
| Submission | Form mapping, TAN flow, receipt checks, state machine | Explicitly stops before bid calculation/submission |
| Observability | JSONL, redaction, replay, SSE dashboard, packaging checks | Console diagnostics and safer excerpts |
| Tests | 81 passing tests, synthetic signed flows and business-rule coverage | No test tree |
| Rehearsal evidence | Two attempted sandbox runs and documented findings | Local exploration diagnosis only |

There is no use of “Clef” in Vlad’s branch. For visual CAPTCHA/verification handling, it captures a masked screenshot and asks Qwen to choose an observed control; it permits a model-selected drag on an observed slider. That is not an external quick-decision/CAPTCHA service. `fresh-start` already has screenshot-grounded interaction, while Vlad’s prompt wording around verification recovery could be useful inspiration.

The branches are conceptually complementary only in a narrow area:

- Vlad offers useful ideas for richer per-action console logging, explicit blocking-notice handling, and verification-gate prompt guidance.
- `fresh-start` provides the implementation needed to actually resolve, price, sign, and verify the tender.

They are not good candidates for a normal merge. They diverged from the orphan baseline and replace the project’s package, manifest, dependency set, root documentation, and runtime contract. Vlad uses `src/rfq_agent`, four browsers, and a planner-only architecture; `fresh-start` uses `src/atira_agent`, one browser, and the complete workflow. A Git merge would mostly create conflicting or redundant code and could regress the required one-browser design.

My recommendation is to retain `fresh-start` as the base and selectively port small ideas from Vlad—primarily the redacted diagnostic logging and verification-gate guidance—after adapting them to the existing one-browser controller. The current implementation and its known live-test limitations are documented in [REHEARSAL_REPORT.md](C:/Users/alvar/Desktop/EHL_Finale/docs/REHEARSAL_REPORT.md) and [README.md](C:/Users/alvar/Desktop/EHL_Finale/README.md).

| Track | Current capability | Live evidence so far |
|---|---|---|
| Tender portal | Reads positions, prepares form fields, requests/enters TAN, verifies receipt | Reached a real tender and recorded five positions; no live signed receipt yet |
| Supplier/specification portal | Reads Q&A, revisions, scoped amendments, documents, including frames/downloads | Reached it in sandbox; an iframe-modal interaction caused the second run to fail. A generic keyboard recovery was added afterward but is not yet sandbox-verified |

| Mail portal | Searches inbox and archive, resolves authorized messages, retrieves TAN and handles replacement | Fully exercised in synthetic layouts, including archived mail and TAN replacement; not completed end-to-end in a live run |

They do not communicate as separate autonomous workers. The controller moves between the four sites serially, based on each current browser observation. The flow is:

```text
Qwen decision
  → validated browser action on the active tab/frame
  → fresh observation
  → quoted evidence ledger
  → deterministic resolution and pricing
  → tender-form/TAN/receipt workflow
```

The shared state is in-process:

- The evidence ledger holds typed facts with citations, source scope, and conflict/unresolved status.
- The pricing engine reads resolved evidence and produces a deterministic result; it does not ask Qwen to calculate.
- The submission state tracks draft → validated → TAN requested → signing attempted → receipt/failed.
- Telemetry publishes redacted events to JSONL and, locally, the SSE dashboard. It is observational only and does not coordinate work.

So the controller is fairly advanced in code coverage and synthetic workflows, but live progress across the four sites is uneven: tender and supplier discovery have been demonstrated, while ERP and mail are currently proven mainly by mock-site tests.

## My request:
About the 4 agents, question: Isnt that approach better? Since each agent has different specializations and can be built to handle a specific type of site. I just shared this page with you so you can skip trial and error since it explains where the traps are in the test eexamples

Yes—four specialized investigators can be better for speed when the runtime actually provides four browsers. Tender, spec, ERP, and mail have very different navigation patterns and evidence types, so splitting their research can reduce the chance that one long Q&A or mail search consumes the full 20-minute budget.

The tradeoff is coordination. Their outputs are tightly coupled:

- Tender Q&A determines quantities and commercial keys.
- Spec data determines which ERP material can match.
- ERP data and mail rules must be combined for pricing.
- The portal can only be signed after all of that resolves.

Four independent agents therefore need a strict shared evidence contract, conflict resolution, and a coordinator that owns pricing and submission. Otherwise they parallelize browsing but create integration failures at the end.

For this challenge, the best shape is a hybrid:

```text
Coordinator
 ├─ Tender investigator
 ├─ Spec investigator
 ├─ ERP investigator
 └─ Mail investigator
      ↓
shared typed evidence ledger
      ↓
single deterministic pricing + submission owner
```

The current branch is deliberately the one-browser version because your original implementation plan explicitly set `browsers: 1` and “no parallel agent architecture.” I should not change that architecture without your direction, especially since the hosted run manifest presently requests one browser.

The workboard is useful and, since you shared it for this purpose, I can use it to eliminate avoidable scouting mistakes. I would use it to add generic, reusable behavior and synthetic test cases for things such as delayed overlays, nested frames, zero-width text normalization, random transient failures, session expiry, fake controls, archive mail, and TAN freshness.

I would not hard-code its particular tender reference, specific control labels, material numbers, values, or fixed navigation paths. Those are public-test facts and would make the agent weaker on the changing private scenario.

If you want to pivot to the four-browser design, say so explicitly and I can prepare a concrete migration: update the manifest, introduce bounded site investigators and a shared evidence ledger, retain one coordinator for pricing/signing, and preserve the current one-browser workflow as a fallback.

## My request:
Design and implement a multi-agent RFQ system with four autonomous, domain-specialized browser agents and one browserless central orchestrator. Each specialist owns one of Atira's four provided CDP browsers. Use dependency-aware asynchronous execution, structured evidence exchange, deterministic pricing and validation, comprehensive per-agent tracing, and a four-browser live debugging view. 

The system must remain genuinely model-directed, generalize to the unseen private scenario, survive individual agent failures and complete a signed bid under the 20-minute limit. Benchmark this architecture against a simpler sequential baseline. If concurrency introduces more failures than benefits, prioritize reliable completion over agent count.



Also , make use of the website I showed you to avoid unnecesary trial and error

"The architecture I'd build\
Central orchestrator\
Distributes tasks, resolves dependencies, combines findings and coordinates submission\
\
\
Agent 1 — Tender\
Tender reference, quantities, Q&A, amendments, deadlines\
Browser 1\
\
\
Agent 2 — Specifications\
Requirements, drawings, technical revisions, certifications\
Browser 2\
\
\
Agent 3 — ERP\
Material matches, stock, lead times, prices, conditions\
Browser 3\
\
\
Agent 4 — Email\
Approved discounts, superseded emails, TAN retrieval\
Browser 4\
\
\
\
\
Shared deterministic validation and pricing engine\
Python Decimal calculations, evidence checking, stock allocation and bid assembly\
\
\
Final bid submission\
Tender agent fills form, email agent retrieves TAN, orchestrator verifies success\
\
\
That is five logical agents, but only four browsers. The orchestrator doesn't need its own browser, so it respects Atira's maximum of four.



But there's a catch: the four agents aren't entirely independent.

For example, the ERP agent cannot confidently select a hydraulic cylinder until the specification agent has identified the exact technical requirements. Similarly, the email agent cannot safely select an approval without knowing the correct tender reference.

So I would implement dependency-aware parallelism, rather than four agents blindly working at the same time.

## How execution should proceed

Phase 1 — Parallel discovery

All four agents navigate their assigned websites. The tender agent identifies the tender, the specification agent investigates available documents, the ERP agent learns how to search materials, and the email agent locates relevant correspondence.

No agent assumes that a particular record is correct before verifying it.

Phase 2 — Exchange structured findings

Once the tender and technical requirements are resolved, the orchestrator provides the actual requirements to ERP and the tender reference to email.

Each agent publishes structured evidence with its source, revision, timestamp and confidence.

Phase 3 — Calculate and validate

A deterministic Python engine calculates the bid. The orchestrator checks for missing evidence, inconsistent quantities, incorrect discounts and unresolved material matches.

If something doesn't agree, it sends a targeted follow-up task to the appropriate specialist.

Phase 4 — Submit

The tender agent enters the bid, the email agent obtains the signing TAN when needed, and the system verifies that the portal actually accepted the submission.

## Three things I'd be careful about

1\. Don't make four agents compete over the same browser. Assign exactly one Atira-provided browser to each specialist. They can use tabs or frames within that browser.

2\. Don't let agents exchange huge raw histories. Give them typed messages and a shared evidence store. Otherwise, multi-agent communication consumes time and tokens without adding much value.

3\. Avoid unnecessary LLM calls. Qwen allows up to 32 concurrent requests per team, but latency and simulated cost still matter. One specialist making 50 unproductive calls is worse than a well-designed agent making 10.

And I'd add one resilience mechanism: a deadline-aware orchestrator. With a few minutes left, it should stop optional exploration and prioritize validating and submitting whatever complete bid positions are available, rather than timing out with zero.

## The debugging interface becomes even more useful

I'd change your Codex prompt to require a dashboard that looks conceptually like this:

Multi-Agent Debug Monitor

Example layout

Tender

Live browser / screenshot

Reading Q&A

Specifications

Live browser / screenshot

Checking revision

ERP

Live browser / screenshot

Searching materials

Email

Live browser / screenshot

Filtering approvals

Shared event timeline

Elapsed 03:24 / 20:00

00:18 · Tender agent identified candidate tender

01:43 · Specifications revision resolved

02:07 · ERP matching started

03:24 · Pricing evidence pending

Illustrative dashboard, not a screenshot of an implemented system. During Atira test runs, the platform already provides browser viewers, recordings and logs; your own monitor could add per-agent decisions, evidence, dependencies and timing.

One final consideration: Atira's fair-play rules allow several agents and up to four browsers, but each agent still has to make genuine model-directed navigation decisions. A fixed browser script disguised as four agents would still violate the rules."

I’ll replace the one-browser controller with four browser-pinned specialists and a browserless coordinator, while retaining the existing deterministic pricing and signing protections. I’ll use the workboard as scouting input for generic recovery tests and agent prompts, not as a source of fixed scenario values or routes.
